solution:
The term is **diffusion**.

Section 10.3 of this chapter lists it among the characteristic properties of gases : "Gases possess the property of diffusion which is a spontaneous homogenous inter mixing of two or more gases." It is possible because gas molecules are widely separated and are in continuous, random motion, colliding with one another and with the walls of the container.

It is called the **partial pressure** of that gas.

Section 10.5.6 defines it in exactly these words : "The pressure exerted by an individual gas in a mixture of two or more gases is called partial pressure. It is also the pressure that each gas would exert if it were present alone." By Dalton's law the partial pressures of the individual gases add up to the total pressure of the mixture, \(\mathrm{P_{Total}} = \mathrm{P_1} + \mathrm{P_2} + \mathrm{P_3} + \ldots\)

The volume **increases**.

At constant pressure a fixed mass of gas obeys Charles' law, \(\dfrac{\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{T}} = \text{constant}\) (Eq. 10.10), so the volume is directly proportional to the temperature in kelvin. Heating raises \(\mathrm{T}\), and the volume must rise in the same proportion to keep the ratio constant — the chapter puts it as "at constant pressure, gases expand on heating and contract on cooling".

The bubble **grows larger** as it rises, and it is largest just as it reaches the surface.

The water standing above the bubble presses down on it, so the pressure on the bubble is greatest at the sea bed and falls steadily as it rises and less water remains above it. Taking the temperature of the sea water as effectively constant, the trapped methane obeys Boyle's law, \(\mathrm{P_1V_1} = \mathrm{P_2V_2}\) (Eq. 10.3) : pressure and volume vary inversely, so as \(\mathrm{P}\) falls \(\mathrm{V}\) must rise. Halving the pressure on the bubble doubles its volume.

The two scales are related by \(\mathrm{T(K)} = t\ ^\circ\mathrm{C} + 273.15\) (section 10.3, measurable property 4). Adding 273.15 to each value :

a. \(-15 + 273.15 = 258.15\ \mathrm{K}\)

b. \(25 + 273.15 = 298.15\ \mathrm{K}\)

c. \(-197 + 273.15 = 76.15\ \mathrm{K}\)

d. \(273 + 273.15 = 546.15\ \mathrm{K}\)

Note that a kelvin temperature is written without a degree sign, and that every value comes out positive — \(-273.15\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\) is absolute zero, below which no temperature exists.

The conversions needed are the ones listed in section 10.3 : \(1\ \mathrm{Pa} = 1\ \mathrm{N\ m^{-2}}\), \(1\ \mathrm{kPa} = 10^{3}\ \mathrm{Pa}\) and \(1\ \mathrm{atm} = 101325\ \mathrm{Pa}\).

a. \(10\ \mathrm{atm} = 10 \times 101325 = 1013250\ \mathrm{Pa} = 1.01325 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{Pa}\)

b. \(1\ \mathrm{kPa} = 1 \times 10^{3} = 1000\ \mathrm{Pa}\)

c. \(107000\ \mathrm{N\ m^{-2}} = 107000\ \mathrm{Pa} = 1.07 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}\) — the pascal **is** the newton per square metre, so this value needs no arithmetic, only the change of name.

d. \(1\ \mathrm{atm} = 101325\ \mathrm{Pa} = 1.01325 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}\)

a. \(1.5\ \mathrm{atm} = 1.5 \times 101325\ \mathrm{Pa} = 151987.5\ \mathrm{Pa} = 1.519875 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}\)

b. \(89\ \mathrm{kPa} = 89 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{Pa} = 8.9 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{N\ m^{-2}}\), since \(1\ \mathrm{Pa} = 1\ \mathrm{N\ m^{-2}}\).

c. \(1\ \mathrm{bar} = 1.00 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa} = 100\ \mathrm{kPa}\), so \(101.325\ \mathrm{kPa} = \dfrac{101.325}{100} = 1.01325\ \mathrm{bar}\). This reproduces the chapter's own statement that \(1\ \mathrm{atm} = 101.325\ \mathrm{kPa} = 1.01325\ \mathrm{bar}\).

d. \(-100\ ^\circ\mathrm{C} = -100 + 273.15 = 173.15\ \mathrm{K}\)

e. \(1\ \mathrm{atm} = 760\ \mathrm{torr}\), so \(0.124\ \mathrm{torr} = \dfrac{0.124}{760} = 1.632 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{atm}\)

Conversion **(a)**, \(\mathrm{H_2} + \mathrm{Cl_2} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{HCl}\), is the one in accordance with the principle of stoichiometry.

Stoichiometry fixes the proportion in which substances actually combine. In (a) one molecule of hydrogen is supplied for every one molecule of chlorine — exactly the \(1 : 1\) proportion the equation demands — so both reactant boxes are emptied and the product box holds nothing but the two \(\mathrm{HCl}\) molecules formed. Every atom supplied ends up in the product.

In (b) two molecules of hydrogen are supplied to one of chlorine. Chlorine is then the limiting reactant : it can consume only one of the two hydrogen molecules, and the product box accordingly shows two \(\mathrm{HCl}\) molecules **together with one unchanged \(\mathrm{H_2}\) molecule** left over. The amounts taken are not in the combining proportion, so hydrogen is in excess and part of it is wasted.

[Note : both drawings are atom-balanced — scheme (b) shows four hydrogen and two chlorine atoms on each side — so what is being tested is the *proportion in which the reactants are taken*, not the balancing of the equation.]

The gas law involved is **Charles' law**.

The air inside a hot air balloon is heated while the balloon stays open at the bottom, so the air inside remains at the same pressure as the atmosphere outside. Under that condition Charles' law applies : \(\dfrac{\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{T}} = \text{constant}\), so the air expands in direct proportion to its kelvin temperature.

Heating therefore lets the **same mass** of air occupy a **larger volume**. Since density is mass per unit volume, \(d = \dfrac{m}{\mathrm{V}}\), an increase in \(\mathrm{V}\) at fixed \(m\) means the density falls. The chapter states the conclusion directly : "at constant pressure, gases expand on heating and contract on cooling. Thus hot air is less dense than cold air."

The warm, less dense air inside is now lighter than an equal volume of the cooler surrounding air, so the balloon experiences a net upward force and rises.

Read each diagram by asking which quantity is held constant and which two are changing.

**a. Boyle's law.** The label reads *T constant*, and the pressure falls from 1 atm to 0.5 atm while the gas expands. With the temperature and the amount of gas fixed, pressure and volume vary inversely : \(\mathrm{P_1V_1} = \mathrm{P_2V_2}\). Halving the pressure doubles the volume, which is what the taller gas column shows.

**b. Charles' law.** Both cylinders are at 1 atm, so the pressure is constant, and the temperature is raised from 200 K to 600 K. Volume is then directly proportional to the kelvin temperature, \(\dfrac{\mathrm{V_1}}{\mathrm{T_1}} = \dfrac{\mathrm{V_2}}{\mathrm{T_2}}\) ; tripling the temperature triples the volume.

**c. Avogadro's law.** Both cylinders are at 1 bar and the amount of gas changes from 1 mol to 1.5 mol, the volume going from 24.8 L to 37.2 L. At constant temperature and pressure the volume is directly proportional to the number of moles, \(\dfrac{\mathrm{V}}{n} = \text{constant}\) — and indeed \(\dfrac{24.8}{1} = \dfrac{37.2}{1.5} = 24.8\ \mathrm{L\ mol^{-1}}\), the same molar volume in both cylinders.

Work out the new volume in each case first ; the piston then has to be drawn at the height that encloses that volume, with the gas shaded below it.

**a. Pressure 1.0 bar \(\to\) 2.0 bar at constant temperature.** Boyle's law gives \(\mathrm{V_2} = \mathrm{V_1} \times \dfrac{\mathrm{P_1}}{\mathrm{P_2}} = \mathrm{V_1} \times \dfrac{1.0}{2.0} = \dfrac{\mathrm{V_1}}{2}\). Draw the piston pushed **down to half** its original height — the gas is compressed to half its volume.

**b. Temperature 300 K \(\to\) 150 K at constant pressure.** Charles' law gives \(\mathrm{V_2} = \mathrm{V_1} \times \dfrac{\mathrm{T_2}}{\mathrm{T_1}} = \mathrm{V_1} \times \dfrac{150}{300} = \dfrac{\mathrm{V_1}}{2}\). Again draw the piston **down at half** the original height ; cooling to half the kelvin temperature halves the volume.

**c. Temperature 400 K \(\to\) 300 K and pressure 4 bar \(\to\) 3 bar.** Here both variables change, so use the combined gas law \(\dfrac{\mathrm{P_1V_1}}{\mathrm{T_1}} = \dfrac{\mathrm{P_2V_2}}{\mathrm{T_2}}\) :

\(\mathrm{V_2} = \mathrm{V_1} \times \dfrac{\mathrm{P_1}}{\mathrm{P_2}} \times \dfrac{\mathrm{T_2}}{\mathrm{T_1}} = \mathrm{V_1} \times \dfrac{4}{3} \times \dfrac{300}{400} = \mathrm{V_1} \times \dfrac{1200}{1200} = \mathrm{V_1}\)

So draw the piston in **exactly its original position — the volume does not change at all**. The cooling would have contracted the gas by a factor \(3/4\), and the drop in pressure would have expanded it by the reciprocal factor \(4/3\) ; the two effects cancel exactly.

Section 10.3 lists six characteristic physical properties of gases.

1. Gases are lighter than solids and liquids, i.e. they possess lower density.

2. Gases do not possess a fixed volume and shape. They occupy the entire space available and take the shape of the container.

3. Gas molecules are widely separated and are in continuous, random motion. Gases therefore exert pressure equally in all directions, because of the collisions of the molecules with the walls of the container.

4. In the case of gases the intermolecular forces are the weakest of the three states.

5. Gases possess the property of diffusion, which is a spontaneous, homogeneous intermixing of two or more gases.

6. Gases are highly compressible — the chapter attributes this to the actual volume of the molecules being negligible compared with the volume of the container.

**a. Polarizability** — the measure of how easily the electron cloud of an atom is distorted by an applied electric field. Equivalently, it is the ability of a molecule to become polar by redistributing its electrons, i.e. to form a momentary dipole. The more electrons a molecule has and the more spread out its shape, the greater its polarizability and the stronger its London dispersion forces.

**b. Hydrogen bond** — the electrostatic force of attraction between a positively polarised hydrogen atom of one molecule and a highly electronegative atom (which may be negatively charged) of another molecule. The electronegative atoms that form hydrogen bonds are nitrogen, oxygen and fluorine. Hydrogen bonds are stronger than ordinary dipole-dipole and dispersion forces (up to about \(40\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)) but weaker than true covalent or ionic bonds.

**c. Aqueous tension** — the pressure exerted by saturated water vapour, that is, the vapour pressure of water. When a gas is collected over water it is mixed with saturated water vapour, so the pressure of the pure dry gas is obtained as \(\mathrm{P_{Dry\ gas}} = \mathrm{P_{Total}} - \mathrm{P_{aq}}\). Aqueous tension increases with increasing temperature (Table 10.5).

**d. Dipole moment** \((\mu)\) — the product of the magnitude of the charge \((\mathrm{Q})\) and the distance between the centres of the positive and negative charge \((r)\), so \(\mu = \mathrm{Q} \times r\). It is a vector quantity, depicted by a small arrow with its tail at the positive centre and its head pointing towards the negative centre, and its unit is the debye \((\mathrm{D})\).

It would be **easier at the base** of Mount Everest and much harder at the top.

You do not suck a liquid up a straw ; you lower the pressure inside your mouth and the straw, and it is the **atmospheric pressure pressing down on the surface of the liquid in the glass** that pushes the liquid up the straw. The height the liquid can be raised therefore depends on how large that outside pressure is.

Atmospheric pressure is greatest at sea level and falls as one climbs, because less and less of the atmosphere remains above — the chapter's own Q.5 (A) uses exactly this fact when it says of a rising balloon that "as it rises in the air external pressure decreases". At the summit of Everest the atmospheric pressure is only a fraction of its sea-level value, so the pushing force available is far smaller and the same effort in your mouth raises much less water.

At the base the atmospheric pressure is close to \(1\ \mathrm{atm} = 101325\ \mathrm{Pa}\), so drinking through a straw is easy.

The rule the chapter gives is : a nonpolar molecule can experience only London dispersion forces ; a polar molecule experiences dipole-dipole forces as well ; and if hydrogen is bonded directly to nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine, hydrogen bonding operates too. London dispersion forces are present in every molecule.

**a. \(\mathrm{CH_3-OH}\)** (methanol) — the \(\mathrm{O-H}\) group puts a hydrogen atom directly on a strongly electronegative oxygen, so **hydrogen bonding** is present, along with dipole-dipole interaction (the molecule is polar) and London dispersion forces. The hydrogen bonding is the dominant force and is why methanol is a liquid at room temperature.

**b. \(\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH_2}\)** (ethene) — a symmetrical hydrocarbon with a negligible dipole moment, so only **London dispersion forces** operate. With very few electrons these forces are weak, which is why ethene is a gas.

**c. \(\mathrm{CHCl_3}\)** (chloroform) — the three \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond dipoles do not cancel against the single \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bond, so the molecule has a permanent dipole moment : **dipole-dipole interaction** together with London dispersion forces. There is no hydrogen bonding, because its hydrogen is bonded to carbon, which is not one of the strongly electronegative atoms.

**d. \(\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}\)** (dichloromethane) — likewise polar, so **dipole-dipole interaction** together with London dispersion forces, and again no hydrogen bonding.

**\(\mathrm{Ar}\)** — a monatomic noble gas with no dipole moment. Only **London dispersion (van der Waals) forces** are present ; the chapter names "helium and other noble gases" among the substances that show the van der Waals force of attraction, and section 10.2.1 (iv) notes that for inert gases only dispersion forces exist.

**\(\mathrm{Cl_2}\)** — a homonuclear diatomic molecule, so both atoms are identical, there is no electronegativity difference and no dipole. Again only **London dispersion forces**, and the chapter lists the halogens explicitly among such substances. Chlorine's dispersion forces are stronger than argon's because it has more electrons.

**\(\mathrm{CCl_4}\)** — the four \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bonds are individually polar, but they point to the four corners of a regular tetrahedron and their dipoles cancel exactly, leaving the molecule with zero net dipole moment. Only **London dispersion forces** are present ; because the molecule is large and has many electrons these are strong enough to make carbon tetrachloride a liquid.

**\(\mathrm{HNO_3}\)** — a polar molecule carrying an \(\mathrm{O-H}\) group, so its hydrogen sits on a strongly electronegative oxygen. **Hydrogen bonding** is present, together with **dipole-dipole interaction** and London dispersion forces. Of the four substances this is the only one with hydrogen bonding.

| 'A' | 'B' |
|---|---|
| a. Boyle's law | ii. at constant temperature |
| b. Charles' law | iii. at constant pressure |

Boyle's law states that for a fixed mass of a gas **at constant temperature** the pressure varies inversely with the volume, which matches (ii). Charles' law states that **at constant pressure** the volume of a fixed mass of a gas is directly proportional to its temperature in kelvin, which matches (iii).

Entry (i), "at constant pressure and volume", is left unmatched. It corresponds to no law in this chapter : if both the pressure and the volume of a fixed mass of gas were held constant then, by \(\mathrm{PV} = n\mathrm{RT}\), the temperature could not change either, so nothing would vary. Column B deliberately carries one more entry than column A.

**(a) Boyle's law** — For a fixed mass (number of moles \(n\)) of a gas at constant temperature, the pressure \((\mathrm{P})\) of a gas is inversely proportional to the volume \((\mathrm{V})\) of the gas. Equivalently : at constant temperature, the pressure of a fixed amount of a gas varies inversely with its volume.

Mathematically \(\mathrm{P} \propto \dfrac{1}{\mathrm{V}}\), so \(\mathrm{PV} = k_1\) and hence \(\mathrm{P_1V_1} = \mathrm{P_2V_2}\).

**(b) Charles' law** — At constant pressure, the volume of a fixed mass of a gas is directly proportional to its temperature in kelvin.

Mathematically \(\mathrm{V} \propto \mathrm{T}\), so \(\dfrac{\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{T}} = k_2\) and hence \(\dfrac{\mathrm{V_1}}{\mathrm{T_1}} = \dfrac{\mathrm{V_2}}{\mathrm{T_2}}\). The temperature must be the absolute (kelvin) temperature, not the celsius temperature.

| Ideal gas | Real gas |
|---|---|
| Strictly obeys Boyle's law and Charles' law, so \(\dfrac{\mathrm{PV}}{n\mathrm{RT}} = 1\). | Deviates from Boyle's law and Charles' law at high pressure and low temperature ; it obeys them only at low pressure and high temperature, so \(\dfrac{\mathrm{PV}}{n\mathrm{RT}} \neq 1\). |
| Molecular collisions are perfectly elastic. | Molecular collisions are not perfectly elastic. |
| There is no attraction or repulsion between the molecules, so collisions take place without loss of kinetic energy. | Intermolecular attraction is present, so collisions take place with loss of kinetic energy. |
| The actual volume of the molecules is negligible compared with the total volume of the gas. | The actual volume of the individual molecules is significant at high pressure and low temperature. |
| Cannot be liquefied even at low temperature ; it would continue to obey Charles' law and finally occupy zero volume at \(-273\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\). | Undergoes liquefaction at low temperature when cooled and compressed. |
| Such a gas does not exist. | All the gases that exist in nature, such as \(\mathrm{H_2}\), \(\mathrm{O_2}\), \(\mathrm{CO_2}\), \(\mathrm{N_2}\) and \(\mathrm{He}\). |

The difference is summarised by the compressibility factor \(\mathrm{Z} = \dfrac{\mathrm{PV}}{n\mathrm{RT}} = \dfrac{\mathrm{V_{real}}}{\mathrm{V_{ideal}}}\), which is exactly 1 for an ideal gas at every pressure and temperature, and departs from 1 for a real gas.

**Statement.** The total pressure of a mixture of two or more non-reactive gases is the sum of the partial pressures of the individual gases in the mixture. The partial pressure of a gas is the pressure it would exert if it alone occupied the whole container.

**Mathematical expression.** At constant volume and temperature,

\(\mathrm{P_{Total}} = \mathrm{P_1} + \mathrm{P_2} + \mathrm{P_3} + \ldots\)

Each partial pressure can be written from the ideal gas equation as \(\mathrm{P_1} = \dfrac{n_1\mathrm{RT}}{\mathrm{V}}\), \(\mathrm{P_2} = \dfrac{n_2\mathrm{RT}}{\mathrm{V}}\), and so on, so that

\(\mathrm{P_{Total}} = \left(\dfrac{\mathrm{RT}}{\mathrm{V}}\right)(n_1 + n_2 + n_3 + \ldots) = \dfrac{\mathrm{RT}}{\mathrm{V}}\,n_{\mathrm{Total}}\)

Dividing one by the other gives the useful working form in terms of mole fraction \(x_1 = \dfrac{n_1}{n_{\mathrm{Total}}}\) :

\(\dfrac{\mathrm{P_1}}{\mathrm{P_{Total}}} = \dfrac{n_1}{n_{\mathrm{Total}}} = x_1 \qquad \therefore\ \mathrm{P_1} = x_1 \times \mathrm{P_{Total}}\)

That is, the partial pressure of a gas is obtained by multiplying the total pressure of the mixture by the mole fraction of that gas.

**Example.** Take a mixture of \(28\ \mathrm{g}\) of \(\mathrm{N_2}\) and \(8\ \mathrm{g}\) of \(\mathrm{He}\) at a total pressure of \(12\ \mathrm{bar}\).

\(n_{\mathrm{N_2}} = \dfrac{28}{28} = 1\ \mathrm{mol}\), \(n_{\mathrm{He}} = \dfrac{8}{4} = 2\ \mathrm{mol}\), so \(n_{\mathrm{Total}} = 3\ \mathrm{mol}\).

\(x_{\mathrm{N_2}} = \dfrac{1}{3}\) and \(x_{\mathrm{He}} = \dfrac{2}{3}\), hence

\(\mathrm{P_{N_2}} = \dfrac{1}{3} \times 12 = 4\ \mathrm{bar}\) and \(\mathrm{P_{He}} = \dfrac{2}{3} \times 12 = 8\ \mathrm{bar}\).

The two partial pressures add back to \(12\ \mathrm{bar}\), as the law requires. A familiar everyday case is air itself, which is about 78 % nitrogen and 21 % oxygen by volume, so at \(1\ \mathrm{atm}\) the partial pressure of nitrogen is about \(0.78\ \mathrm{atm}\) and that of oxygen about \(0.21\ \mathrm{atm}\).

The law holds only for gases that do **not** react chemically on mixing.

**Derivation.** Write down the three gas laws as proportionalities, each holding while the other variables are fixed :

1. At constant \(\mathrm{T}\) and \(n\) : \(\mathrm{V} \propto \dfrac{1}{\mathrm{P}}\)  (Boyle's law)

2. At constant \(\mathrm{P}\) and \(n\) : \(\mathrm{V} \propto \mathrm{T}\)  (Charles' law)

3. At constant \(\mathrm{P}\) and \(\mathrm{T}\) : \(\mathrm{V} \propto n\)  (Avogadro's law)

Combining all three,

\(\mathrm{V} \propto \dfrac{n\mathrm{T}}{\mathrm{P}}\)

Introducing a constant of proportionality \(\mathrm{R}\) turns the proportionality into an equation,

\(\mathrm{V} = \mathrm{R}\left(\dfrac{n\mathrm{T}}{\mathrm{P}}\right) \qquad \therefore\ \mathrm{PV} = n\mathrm{RT}\)

This is the **ideal gas equation**. Because it fixes the state of the gas, it is also called the equation of state ; if any three of the four variables are known the fourth can be calculated.

**Terms involved.**

\(\mathrm{P}\) = pressure of the gas (SI unit pascal, \(\mathrm{Pa}\))

\(\mathrm{V}\) = volume of the gas (SI unit \(\mathrm{m^3}\) ; commonly \(\mathrm{dm^3}\) or L)

\(n\) = number of moles of the gas

\(\mathrm{T}\) = absolute temperature in kelvin

\(\mathrm{R}\) = the gas constant. Its value is the same for all gases, so it is called the **universal gas constant** ; its numerical value depends only on the units chosen — \(8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\) in SI units, \(0.0821\ \mathrm{dm^3\ atm\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\) with pressure in atmospheres, or about \(2\ \mathrm{cal\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\).

**Obtaining the combined gas law.** Rearranging the ideal gas equation,

\(\dfrac{\mathrm{PV}}{\mathrm{T}} = n\mathrm{R} = \text{constant}\)

For a **fixed amount** of gas, \(n\) does not change and \(\mathrm{R}\) never does, so the whole right-hand side is a constant. Writing the same gas in two different states therefore gives

\(\dfrac{\mathrm{P_1V_1}}{\mathrm{T_1}} = \dfrac{\mathrm{P_2V_2}}{\mathrm{T_2}}\)

which is the **combined gas law**. Boyle's, Charles' and Gay-Lussac's laws are each recovered from it by holding one of the three variables constant.

The graph is a plot of pressure \(\mathrm{P}\) against \(\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{V}}\), marked *T constant*. It is a **straight line passing through the origin**.

**a. The relation, mathematically.** A straight line through the origin means the two plotted quantities are directly proportional, so

\(\mathrm{P} \propto \dfrac{1}{\mathrm{V}} \qquad \therefore\ \mathrm{P} = k_1 \dfrac{1}{\mathrm{V}} \qquad \therefore\ \mathrm{PV} = k_1 = \text{constant}\)

and for the same gas in two states, \(\mathrm{P_1V_1} = \mathrm{P_2V_2}\). The slope of the line is the constant \(k_1\), whose value depends only on the temperature and the amount of gas.

**b. The law.** This is **Boyle's law**. (Had the plot instead been volume against kelvin temperature it would have been Charles' law ; the giveaway here is that the temperature is held constant while the pressure and volume both change.)

**c. Statement of the law.** For a fixed mass (number of moles \(n\)) of a gas at constant temperature, the pressure of the gas is inversely proportional to its volume — or equivalently, at constant temperature the pressure of a fixed amount of a gas varies inversely with its volume.

Section 10.6 gives seven assumptions of the kinetic molecular theory of gases.

1. Gases consist of tiny particles (molecules or atoms).

2. On an average the gas molecules remain far apart from one another, so the actual volume of the gas particles is negligible compared with the volume of the container. This is why gases are highly compressible.

3. The attractive forces between the gas molecules are negligible at ordinary temperature and pressure. As a result a gas expands to occupy the entire volume of its container.

4. Gas molecules are in constant random motion and move in all possible directions in straight lines. They collide with one another and with the walls of the container.

5. The pressure of the gas is due to the collisions of the gas particles with the walls of the container.

6. The collisions of the gas molecules are perfectly elastic in nature, which means that the total energy of the gaseous particles remains unchanged after a collision.

7. Different molecules of a gas move with different velocities at any instant and so have different kinetic energies, but the **average** kinetic energy of the molecules is directly proportional to the absolute temperature :

\(\text{Average K.E.} \propto \mathrm{T}\)

**a. Vapour pressure.** Molecules of a liquid tend to escape from its surface to form vapour above it — evaporation. When a liquid is placed in a closed container, evaporation and the condensation of the vapour both proceed until, at equilibrium, their rates become equal. The pressure exerted by the vapour that is then in equilibrium with its liquid is called the saturated vapour pressure, or simply the **vapour pressure**. The vapour pressure of water is also called aqueous tension.

Two factors govern it. *Nature of the liquid* : liquids with relatively weak intermolecular forces have high vapour pressures and are called volatile liquids — petrol evaporates much faster than motor oil. *Temperature* : heating a liquid raises its vapour pressure. When the vapour pressure becomes equal to the pressure above the liquid, the liquid boils. It is measured with a manometer, and its commonest unit is the torr \((1\ \mathrm{torr} = 1\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg})\) ; water has a vapour pressure of roughly 20 torr at room temperature.

**b. Surface tension.** A molecule in the bulk of a liquid is pulled equally in all directions, so the net force on it is zero ; a molecule at the surface has no liquid above it and experiences a net inward pull towards the interior. The surface therefore behaves like a stretched membrane and the liquid tends to minimise its surface area, which is why drops are spherical and why liquids rise in a capillary.

**Surface tension is the force acting per unit length perpendicular to a line drawn on the surface of the liquid.** Its SI unit is \(\mathrm{N\ m^{-1}}\) and it is denoted by \(\gamma\) (gamma). It is temperature dependent : raising the temperature increases the kinetic energy of the molecules, weakens the intermolecular attraction, and so **decreases** the surface tension. Its applications include the cleaning action of soaps and detergents, which lower the interfacial tension between water and oily matter so that the solution can penetrate the fibre, and the penetrating action of toothpastes, mouthwashes and nasal drops.

**c. Viscosity.** When a liquid flows, different layers move with different velocities — laminar flow. The layer in immediate contact with a fixed surface stays stationary and the layers above slip over one another, strong intermolecular forces obstructing the slipping and producing friction between the layers.

**Viscosity is the force of friction between the successive layers of a flowing liquid**, that is, the resistance to the flow of the liquid. It is expressed through the coefficient of viscosity \(\eta\) (eta), whose SI unit is \(\mathrm{N\ s\ m^{-2}}\) ; in the CGS system it is measured in poise, \(1\ \text{poise} = 1\ \mathrm{g\ cm^{-1}\ s^{-1}} = 10^{-1}\ \mathrm{kg\ m^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\).

Viscosity falls as the temperature rises \(\left(\eta \propto \dfrac{1}{\text{Temperature}}\right)\), and it also depends on molecular size and shape : larger molecules are more viscous, while spherical molecules offer the least resistance to flow. The greater the viscosity, the slower the liquid flows. Lubricating oils are graded by viscosity, a rise in blood viscosity above normal is taken as an indication of cardiovascular disease, and the thickening of old window panes near the bottom is evidence that glass is a supercooled viscous liquid rather than a true solid.

The helium is a fixed mass of gas and the temperature is taken as constant, so Boyle's law applies : \(\mathrm{P_1V_1} = \mathrm{P_2V_2}\).

Given : \(\mathrm{P_1} = 1\ \mathrm{bar}\), \(\mathrm{V_1} = 2.27\ \mathrm{L}\), \(\mathrm{P_2} = 0.3\ \mathrm{bar}\), \(\mathrm{V_2} = ?\)

\(\mathrm{V_2} = \dfrac{\mathrm{P_1V_1}}{\mathrm{P_2}} = \dfrac{1\ \mathrm{bar} \times 2.27\ \mathrm{L}}{0.3\ \mathrm{bar}} = 7.567\ \mathrm{L}\)

The balloon can stay inflated up to a volume of about \(7.567\ \mathrm{L}\) ; beyond that it bursts. The volume has risen because the external pressure fell — the pressure dropped to less than a third of its starting value, so the volume grew by more than a factor of three.

Plugging the end traps a fixed mass of gas and the temperature does not change, so Boyle's law applies : \(\mathrm{P_1V_1} = \mathrm{P_2V_2}\).

Given : \(\mathrm{P_1} = 1\ \mathrm{atm}\), \(\mathrm{V_1} = 10.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}\), \(\mathrm{P_2} = 3.5\ \mathrm{atm}\), \(\mathrm{V_2} = ?\)

\(\mathrm{V_2} = \dfrac{\mathrm{P_1V_1}}{\mathrm{P_2}} = \dfrac{1\ \mathrm{atm} \times 10.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}}{3.5\ \mathrm{atm}} = 2.857\ \mathrm{cm^3} \approx 2.9\ \mathrm{cm^3}\)

The plunger must be pushed in until the gas occupies about \(2.9\ \mathrm{cm^3}\). The pressure is raised 3.5 times, so the volume is reduced to \(1/3.5\) of its original value.

The pressure is constant and the mass of gas is fixed, so Charles' law applies : \(\dfrac{\mathrm{V_1}}{\mathrm{T_1}} = \dfrac{\mathrm{V_2}}{\mathrm{T_2}}\), with the temperatures in kelvin.

Initial state : \(\mathrm{V_1} = 2\ \mathrm{dm^3}\) at \(0\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\), so \(\mathrm{T_1} = 0 + 273.15 = 273.15\ \mathrm{K}\).

**a. Temperature increased by \(10\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\)**, so \(\mathrm{T_2} = 10 + 273.15 = 283.15\ \mathrm{K}\) :

\(\mathrm{V_2} = \dfrac{\mathrm{V_1}\mathrm{T_2}}{\mathrm{T_1}} = \dfrac{2 \times 283.15}{273.15} = 2.073\ \mathrm{dm^3}\)

The volume **increases** to about \(2.07\ \mathrm{dm^3}\).

**b. Temperature decreased by \(10\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\)**, so \(\mathrm{T_2} = -10 + 273.15 = 263.15\ \mathrm{K}\) :

\(\mathrm{V_2} = \dfrac{2 \times 263.15}{273.15} = 1.927\ \mathrm{dm^3}\)

The volume **decreases** to about \(1.93\ \mathrm{dm^3}\).

Notice that a \(10\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\) change alters the volume by only about 3.7 %, because \(10\ \mathrm{K}\) is a small fraction of \(273.15\ \mathrm{K}\). Working in celsius instead of kelvin would have given a nonsensical answer, since \(\mathrm{V_1}/0\) is undefined.

A hot air balloon is open to the atmosphere, so the pressure is constant and Charles' law applies : \(\dfrac{\mathrm{V_1}}{\mathrm{T_1}} = \dfrac{\mathrm{V_2}}{\mathrm{T_2}}\).

Given : \(\mathrm{V_1} = 2800\ \mathrm{m^3}\), \(\mathrm{T_1} = 99 + 273.15 = 372.15\ \mathrm{K}\), \(\mathrm{T_2} = 80 + 273.15 = 353.15\ \mathrm{K}\), \(\mathrm{V_2} = ?\)

\(\mathrm{V_2} = \dfrac{\mathrm{V_1}\mathrm{T_2}}{\mathrm{T_1}} = \dfrac{2800\ \mathrm{m^3} \times 353.15\ \mathrm{K}}{372.15\ \mathrm{K}} = 2657\ \mathrm{m^3}\)

The volume **decreases** to about \(2657\ \mathrm{m^3}\), a contraction of roughly 143 \(\mathrm{m^3}\), because the air has been cooled.

The pressure is not changed and the mass of gas is fixed, so Charles' law applies : \(\dfrac{\mathrm{V_1}}{\mathrm{T_1}} = \dfrac{\mathrm{V_2}}{\mathrm{T_2}}\).

Given : \(\mathrm{V_1} = 22.4\ \mathrm{L}\), \(\mathrm{T_1} = 0 + 273.15 = 273.15\ \mathrm{K}\), \(\mathrm{V_2} = 25.0\ \mathrm{L}\), \(\mathrm{T_2} = ?\)

\(\mathrm{T_2} = \dfrac{\mathrm{V_2}\mathrm{T_1}}{\mathrm{V_1}} = \dfrac{25.0\ \mathrm{L} \times 273.15\ \mathrm{K}}{22.4\ \mathrm{L}} = 304.85\ \mathrm{K}\)

In celsius : \(t_2 = 304.85 - 273.15 = 31.70\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\)

So the gas must be heated to about \(304.9\ \mathrm{K}\), that is \(31.7\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\) — a rise of \(31.7\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\) above the starting temperature, since the gas began at \(0\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\).

Here the pressure, the volume, the temperature **and** the amount of gas all change, so neither Boyle's nor Charles' law is enough on its own. Start from \(\mathrm{PV} = n\mathrm{RT}\) and note that \(\dfrac{\mathrm{PV}}{n\mathrm{T}} = \mathrm{R}\) is the same constant in both states :

\(\dfrac{\mathrm{P_1V_1}}{n_1\mathrm{T_1}} = \dfrac{\mathrm{P_2V_2}}{n_2\mathrm{T_2}} \qquad \therefore\ \mathrm{P_2} = \mathrm{P_1} \times \dfrac{\mathrm{V_1}}{\mathrm{V_2}} \times \dfrac{\mathrm{T_2}}{\mathrm{T_1}} \times \dfrac{n_2}{n_1}\)

Given : \(\mathrm{P_1} = 628.3\ \mathrm{bar}\), \(\mathrm{V_1} = 20\ \mathrm{L}\), \(n_1 = 0.650\ \mathrm{mol}\), \(\mathrm{T_1} = 37 + 273.15 = 310.15\ \mathrm{K}\) ; \(\mathrm{V_2} = 12\ \mathrm{L}\), \(\mathrm{T_2} = 177 + 273.15 = 450.15\ \mathrm{K}\), and the added gas makes \(n_2 = 0.650 + 1.25 = 1.90\ \mathrm{mol}\).

\(\mathrm{P_2} = 628.3 \times \dfrac{20}{12} \times \dfrac{450.15}{310.15} \times \dfrac{1.90}{0.650}\)

\(= 628.3 \times 1.6667 \times 1.4514 \times 2.9231 = 4442.6\ \mathrm{bar}\)

Converting, \(1\ \mathrm{atm} = 1.01325\ \mathrm{bar}\), so

\(\mathrm{P_2} = \dfrac{4442.6}{1.01325} = 4384.5\ \mathrm{atm}\)

The new pressure is about \(4443\ \mathrm{bar}\), or about \(4385\ \mathrm{atm}\). Every one of the three changes raises the pressure — the volume is reduced, the temperature is raised and more gas is added — so a large increase is expected.

[Note : the pressures here are extreme, and the initial state as given is not itself consistent with the ideal gas equation — \(0.650\ \mathrm{mol}\) of helium in \(20\ \mathrm{L}\) at \(310.15\ \mathrm{K}\) would exert only about \(0.84\ \mathrm{bar}\), not \(628.3\ \mathrm{bar}\). The question is nonetheless answerable exactly as set, because the combined-law route uses only the **ratios** of the four quantities and never needs the absolute value of \(\mathrm{R}\).]

Use the ideal gas equation \(\mathrm{PV} = n\mathrm{RT}\), rearranged as \(n = \dfrac{\mathrm{PV}}{\mathrm{RT}}\) (Eq. 10.16).

The pressure is in atmospheres and the volume in litres, so take \(\mathrm{R} = 0.0821\ \mathrm{dm^3\ atm\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\) — the units must match, or the answer will be wrong by orders of magnitude.

Given : \(\mathrm{P} = 4.7\ \mathrm{atm}\), \(\mathrm{V} = 2.32\ \mathrm{L} = 2.32\ \mathrm{dm^3}\), \(\mathrm{T} = 32 + 273.15 = 305.15\ \mathrm{K}\)

\(n = \dfrac{4.7 \times 2.32}{0.0821 \times 305.15} = \dfrac{10.904}{25.053} = 0.435\ \mathrm{mol}\)

The container holds about \(0.435\ \mathrm{mol}\) of nitrogen — roughly \(0.435 \times 28 = 12.2\ \mathrm{g}\).

[Note : the book prints \(0.436\) mol. The difference is only in the value taken for the gas constant : \(\mathrm{R} = 0.0820\) gives \(0.436\) and \(\mathrm{R} = 0.0821\), the value in the chapter's own Table 10.4, gives \(0.435\). Either is acceptable to three significant figures.]

The mass of gas is fixed while the pressure, volume and temperature all change, so use the combined gas law : \(\dfrac{\mathrm{P_1V_1}}{\mathrm{T_1}} = \dfrac{\mathrm{P_2V_2}}{\mathrm{T_2}}\).

Given : \(\mathrm{P_1} = 760\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}\), \(\mathrm{V_1} = 600\ \mathrm{mL}\), \(\mathrm{T_1} = 25 + 273.15 = 298.15\ \mathrm{K}\) ; \(\mathrm{V_2} = 640\ \mathrm{mL}\), \(\mathrm{T_2} = 10 + 273.15 = 283.15\ \mathrm{K}\), \(\mathrm{P_2} = ?\)

\(\mathrm{P_2} = \dfrac{\mathrm{P_1V_1T_2}}{\mathrm{T_1V_2}} = \dfrac{760 \times 600 \times 283.15}{298.15 \times 640} = 676.7\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}\)

The pressure at that height is about \(676.6\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}\). The volumes need no conversion to litres because they appear as a ratio, and the pressure comes out in whatever unit \(\mathrm{P_1}\) was given in. The result is a fall in pressure, as expected — both the expansion of the gas and the drop in temperature act to lower it.

By Dalton's law the partial pressure of a gas is its mole fraction times the total pressure, \(\mathrm{P_i} = x_i \times \mathrm{P_{Total}}\) (Eq. 10.27). So first find the moles of each gas.

**Step 1 — moles.** Molar masses : \(\mathrm{O_2} = 32\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\), \(\mathrm{Ne} = 20.18\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\).

\(n_{\mathrm{O_2}} = \dfrac{70.6\ \mathrm{g}}{32\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 2.206\ \mathrm{mol}\)

\(n_{\mathrm{Ne}} = \dfrac{167.5\ \mathrm{g}}{20.18\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 8.300\ \mathrm{mol}\)

\(n_{\mathrm{Total}} = 2.206 + 8.300 = 10.506\ \mathrm{mol}\)

**Step 2 — mole fractions.**

\(x_{\mathrm{O_2}} = \dfrac{2.206}{10.506} = 0.2100\) and \(x_{\mathrm{Ne}} = \dfrac{8.300}{10.506} = 0.7900\)

(The two mole fractions add to 1, which is the check on this step.)

**Step 3 — partial pressures.**

\(\mathrm{P_{O_2}} = 0.2100 \times 25\ \mathrm{bar} = 5.25\ \mathrm{bar}\)

\(\mathrm{P_{Ne}} = 0.7900 \times 25\ \mathrm{bar} = 19.75\ \mathrm{bar}\)

The two partial pressures add back to \(25\ \mathrm{bar}\), as Dalton's law requires. Note that neon supplies the larger partial pressure although the masses are of the same order — what counts is the **number of molecules**, and neon's small molar mass means \(167.5\ \mathrm{g}\) of it contains nearly four times as many moles as \(70.6\ \mathrm{g}\) of dioxygen.

[Note : rounding neon's molar mass to \(20\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\) instead of \(20.18\) shifts the answers only slightly, to \(5.21\ \mathrm{bar}\) and \(19.79\ \mathrm{bar}\).]

Use the ideal gas equation \(\mathrm{PV} = n\mathrm{RT}\), rearranged as \(\mathrm{P} = \dfrac{n\mathrm{RT}}{\mathrm{V}}\).

The answer is wanted in atmospheres and the volume is in \(\mathrm{dm^3}\), so take \(\mathrm{R} = 0.0821\ \mathrm{dm^3\ atm\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\).

Given : \(n = 1.0\ \mathrm{mol}\), \(\mathrm{V} = 2.0\ \mathrm{dm^3}\), \(\mathrm{T} = 20.0 + 273.15 = 293.15\ \mathrm{K}\)

\(\mathrm{P} = \dfrac{1.0 \times 0.0821 \times 293.15}{2.0} = \dfrac{24.068}{2.0} = 12.03\ \mathrm{atm}\)

The pressure is about \(12.03\ \mathrm{atm}\). Nothing in the calculation depends on the gas being helium — an ideal gas of any identity at the same \(n\), \(\mathrm{V}\) and \(\mathrm{T}\) would exert the same pressure.

[Note : the book prints \(12.02\ \mathrm{atm}\), which is what the more precise \(\mathrm{R} = 0.08206\) gives \((12.028)\). The chapter's own Table 10.4 value \(0.0821\) gives \(12.034\) ; the two agree to three significant figures.]

Use \(\mathrm{PV} = n\mathrm{RT}\), rearranged as \(\mathrm{V} = \dfrac{n\mathrm{RT}}{\mathrm{P}}\).

The pressure is given in kilopascals, so work in SI units with \(\mathrm{R} = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\) and the pressure in pascals ; the volume then comes out in \(\mathrm{m^3}\).

Given : \(n = 1\ \mathrm{mol}\), \(\mathrm{T} = 20 + 273.15 = 293.15\ \mathrm{K}\), \(\mathrm{P} = 101.35\ \mathrm{kPa} = 101350\ \mathrm{Pa}\)

\(\mathrm{V} = \dfrac{1 \times 8.314 \times 293.15}{101350} = \dfrac{2437.2}{101350} = 0.02405\ \mathrm{m^3}\)

Converting, \(1\ \mathrm{m^3} = 10^{3}\ \mathrm{dm^3}\), so

\(\mathrm{V} = 0.02405 \times 10^{3} = 24.05\ \mathrm{dm^3}\)

One mole of the gas occupies about \(24.05\ \mathrm{dm^3}\) under these conditions. This is sensibly larger than the molar volume of \(22.71\ \mathrm{L\ mol^{-1}}\) at STP, because the temperature here is about 20 K above \(273.15\ \mathrm{K}\) while the pressure is close to 1 bar.

[Note : the book prints \(24.055\ \mathrm{dm^3}\). That value follows from taking the pressure as exactly \(101.325\ \mathrm{kPa}\), i.e. 1 atmosphere, rather than the \(101.35\ \mathrm{kPa}\) the question states ; using the stated figure gives \(24.048\ \mathrm{dm^3}\). The two differ by 0.03 % and round to the same value at four significant figures.]

Find the number of moles from the ideal gas equation first, then convert moles to molecules with the Avogadro number.

**Step 1 — moles.** \(n = \dfrac{\mathrm{PV}}{\mathrm{RT}}\), working in SI units with \(\mathrm{R} = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\), the pressure in pascals and the volume in \(\mathrm{m^3}\).

Given : \(\mathrm{P} = 2.0 \times 10^{2}\ \mathrm{kPa} = 2.0 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}\), \(\mathrm{V} = 0.50\ \mathrm{m^3}\), \(\mathrm{T} = 300\ \mathrm{K}\)

\(n = \dfrac{2.0 \times 10^{5} \times 0.50}{8.314 \times 300} = \dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{5}}{2494.2} = 40.09\ \mathrm{mol}\)

**Step 2 — molecules.** One mole contains \(\mathrm{N_A} = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\) molecules, so

\(\mathrm{N} = n \times \mathrm{N_A} = 40.09 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 2.414 \times 10^{25}\)

There are about \(2.4 \times 10^{25}\) molecules of methane in the sample. Note that the identity of the gas never enters the calculation — by Avogadro's law any ideal gas would give the same count under the same conditions.
